title: Signal Processing
body:
We rely on signals such as sound and images to convey information. Signal processing is the field concerned with analysing, generating, and transforming signals. Its applications can be found in a wide range of fields: audio processing, speech recognition, image processing, communication systems, data science, etc. In this chapter we focus on Fourier Transform, the fundamental tool in signal processing and modern numerical computing. We introduce its basic idea, and then demonstrate how to perform FFT in OCaml with examples and applications. We also cover the relationship between FFT, convolution, and filters.

Running the examples

Source: code/chap07_signal
Run: python3 scripts/run_chapter07.py

In utop, load this setup, including the frequency-axis and inverse-transform helpers, then follow the examples in order:

OCAML
open Owl_plplot;;
Owl_stats_prng.init 77;;
let book_matrix_printer formatter value =
  Owl_pretty.print_dsnda ~max_row:6 ~max_col:6 ~formatter value;;
#install_printer book_matrix_printer;;
Sys.chdir "/opt/book/code/chap07_signal";;
#use "book_signal.ml";;

The image example uses double precision to avoid a single-precision complex FFT bytecode defect in the recorded Owl revision.

For the second edition, the three CSV inputs are reproducible synthetic teaching data generated by generate_inputs.py. The historical filenames are retained, but these files contain no measured solar observations, recorded phone call, or real Google prices.

7.1 Discrete Fourier Transform

We begin with an example. Consider a piece of audio lasting 10 seconds. It can clearly be described in the time domain by plotting its sound pressure against time. On the other hand, perhaps less obviously, it can also be described in the frequency domain. For example, an ideal sinusoidal tone at A#4 has a frequency of about 466.16 Hz in equal temperament with A4 tuned to 440 Hz. Its amplitude, phase and duration are also needed to describe the signal. Of course, real-world sounds such as water flowing or wind whispering are not usually so pure, typically being compounded from different frequencies. How should we describe the frequencies used then?

That’s where the Fourier Transform comes in, starting from a fundamental insight: all signals, whether sound waves or electromagnetic fields, can be described as a waveform, and under suitable conditions, waveforms can be represented by sums or integrals of sinusoids of different frequencies [21]. The Fourier Transform is the tool to break down a signal wave into different sinusoids.

More formally, we can represent a signal with the values of some quantity h as a function of time: h(t), or its complex spectrum H(f), which contains amplitude and phase information as a function of frequency. They are two representations of the same thing, and the Fourier Transform converts between them as shown in Eq. 7.1. These two equations show the Fourier transform, and the inverse Fourier transform [2], which changes a signal from the frequency domain back to the time domain.

H(f) = ∫ −∞∞h(t)e−2𝜋𝑖𝑓𝑡𝑑𝑡 h(t) = ∫ −∞∞H(f)e2𝜋𝑖𝑓𝑡𝑑𝑓 (7.1)

In computer-based numerical computation, signals are often represented discretely as a finite sequence of sampled data rather than as continuous values, giving rise to the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) [3]. Suppose we have represented a signal by a complex vector y that contains n elements. To get the Fourier Transform vector Y , the DFT and its inverse are given in Eq. 7.2, where ω = e−2𝜋𝑖∕n and i = −1. j and k are indices that range from 0 to n − 1. 1

Y k = ∑ j=0n−1y jω𝑗𝑘 yj = 1 n∑ k=0n−1Y kω−𝑗𝑘 (7.2)

What can we do if we know how a sound is composed? Think of a classic example where we need to reduce high-pitched noise in some music. If the noise occupies frequencies that can be separated from the music, we can attenuate those components in the frequency domain and convert the signal back to the time domain using the inverse Fourier transform. Similarly, we can reduce noise in an image by filtering its frequency components before inverting the transform. Filtering can also remove useful detail when signal and noise occupy the same frequencies. We show several such examples in Sec. 7.3.

There are many many more applications of DFT than just de-noising though [4]. We all use Fourier Transform every day without knowing it: mobile phones [5], image and audio compression [6], communication networks [7], large scale numerical physics and engineering [8], etc. In many ways it is the cornerstone of computational mathematics. An important reason for its popularity is that it can be implemented very efficiently as the Fast Fourier Transform.

7.2 Fast Fourier Transform

A problem with the DFT is that if you follow its definition in implementation, the computational complexity of your algorithm is 𝒪(n2): computing each of the n components of Y in Eq. 7.2 requires n multiplications and n additions. Therefore naive DFT implementation does not scale well with input size. Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithms reduce this complexity to 𝒪(nlog⁡n). An early form is found in work by Gauss dating from around 1805; the publication by James Cooley and John Tukey in 1965 made the approach widely known [9]. In the radix-2 case, with n a power of two, the DFT can be split into two sub-DFTs: one consisting of the elements of the signal in the even index positions, and the other consisting of the elements of the signal in odd positions:

Y k = ∑ 𝑒𝑣𝑒𝑛𝑗ω𝑗𝑘y j + ∑ 𝑜𝑑𝑑𝑗ω𝑗𝑘y j = ∑ j=0n∕2−1ω2𝑗𝑘y 2j + ωk ∑ j=0n∕2−1ω2𝑗𝑘y 2j+1. (7.3)

The key to enabling this step is the fact that ω2n2 = ωn. According to Eq. 7.3, one DFT can be reduced into two DFTs each only half the original length, and then the second half is multiplied by a factor ωk and added to the first half. The half signal can be further halved, and so on and so on. There are logarithmically many recursion levels, with linear work at each level. At the base of this recursion is the fact that a DFT on a single number returns just the number itself. As you can see, this is a typical divide-and-conquer algorithm design.

Detailed mathematical analysis of the Fourier Transform is beyond the scope of this book, and we encourage readers to consult one of the many classic textbooks on this topic such as Phillips et al [10]. We focus here on introducing how to use the FFT implementation and its applications in OCaml code. Hopefully these materials are interesting enough to encourage you to investigate more.

The implementation of the FFT module in the Owl library uses the PocketFFT [11] C++ backend. The core functions in the FFT module are fft and its inverse ifft, corresponding to the two equations in Eq. 7.2. Tbl. 7.1 lists the basic functions in Owl_fft.D, used below. Their inputs are ndarrays. The FFT module provides S and D submodules for single and double precision, each handling the corresponding real and complex array types, and a Generic interface. The optional axis selects the array axis to transform and defaults to the last axis. For irfft, n specifies the real output length along that axis. With the defaults used here, the forward transform is unscaled and the inverse is divided by the transform length.

7.2.1 Example: 1-D Discrete Fourier Transforms

We next show how to use these functions with some simple examples. More complex and interesting ones will follow in the next section.

Let’s start with the most basic fft and its inverse transform function ifft. First, we create a complex 1-D ndarray that contains 6 elements as input to fft.

OCAML SESSION
# let a = [|1.;2.;1.;-1.;1.5;1.0|];;
val a : float array = [|1.; 2.; 1.; -1.; 1.5; 1.|]
# let b = Arr.of_array a [|6|]
    |> Dense.Ndarray.Generic.cast_d2z;;
val b : (Complex.t, Bigarray.complex64_elt) Owl.Dense.Ndarray.Generic.t =

       C0      C1      C2       C3        C4      C5
R (1, 0i) (2, 0i) (1, 0i) (-1, 0i) (1.5, 0i) (1, 0i)

We then apply the FFT:

OCAML SESSION
# let c = Owl_fft.D.fft b;;
val c : (Complex.t, Bigarray.complex64_elt) Owl_dense_ndarray_generic.t =

         C0                 C1                 C2        C3                C4                C5
R (5.5, 0i) (2.25, -0.433013i) (-2.75, -1.29904i) (1.5, 0i) (-2.75, 1.29904i) (2.25, 0.433013i)

The input and output of fft are both complex ndarrays. When the original samples are real, as here, the spectrum has conjugate symmetry: Y n−k = Y k¯ for 1 ≤ k < n. Its magnitude is therefore symmetric between positive and negative frequencies; this is not true for arbitrary complex input. Bin zero is the DC component, followed by positive-frequency bins and then negative-frequency bins in wrapped order. For even n, bin n∕2 is the Nyquist component. For real input, the nonnegative-frequency half-spectrum is sufficient for plotting, but reconstruction must also account for its conjugate half.

OCAML SESSION
# let d = Owl_fft.D.ifft c;;
val d : (Complex.t, Bigarray.complex64_elt) Owl_dense_ndarray_generic.t =

       C0      C1      C2       C3        C4      C5
R (1, 0i) (2, 0i) (1, 0i) (-1, 0i) (1.5, 0i) (1, 0i)

The function ifft takes the frequency domain result c produced by fft and reconstructs the original time domain signal. Since we do not change the frequencies generated by fft, the inverse FFT should recover the original input up to floating-point round-off, as in this example.

But simply manipulating arrays does not make very impressive examples. We next plot the FFT of the sum of two sine waves showing the power of FFT to separate signals of different frequencies. This example uses 600 sampling points and the sample spacing is 1 800 seconds.

OCAML SESSION
# module G = Dense.Ndarray.Generic;;
module G = Owl.Dense.Ndarray.Generic
# let n = 600.;;
val n : float = 600.
# let t = 1. /. 800.;;
val t : float = 0.00125
# let x = Arr.mul_scalar (Arr.sequential [|int_of_float n|]) t;;
val x : Owl.Arr.arr =

  C0      C1     C2        C597   C598    C599
R  0 0.00125 0.0025 ... 0.74625 0.7475 0.74875

First, we create 600 sample times in [0,0.75) seconds, with a step size of 0.00125 seconds; the last sample is at 0.74875 seconds.

OCAML SESSION
# let y1 = Arr.((50. *. 2. *. Owl_const.pi) $* x |> sin);;
val y1 : Owl.Arr.arr =

  C0       C1       C2        C597     C598     C599
R  0 0.382683 0.707107 ... 0.92388 0.707107 0.382683
# let y2 = Arr.(0.5 $* ((80. *. 2. *. Owl_const.pi)
    $* x |> sin));;
val y2 : (float, Bigarray.float64_elt) Owl_dense_ndarray_generic.t =

  C0       C1       C2          C597      C598      C599
R  0 0.293893 0.475528 ... -0.475528 -0.475528 -0.293893

Next we create two sine signals of different frequencies: y1(x) = sin⁡(100𝜋𝑥), y2(x) = 1 2 sin⁡(160𝜋𝑥), at 50 and 80 Hz respectively, shown in Fig. 7.1a. We then mix them together.

OCAML SESSION
# let y = Arr.(y1 + y2) |> G.cast_d2z;;
val y : (Complex.t, Bigarray.complex64_elt) G.t =

       C0             C1            C2               C597           C598            C599
R (0, 0i) (0.676576, 0i) (1.18264, 0i) ... (0.448351, 0i) (0.231579, 0i) (0.0887908, 0i)

The combined signal in Fig. 7.1b shows an irregular shape. Next, we apply FFT on this mixed signal:

OCAML SESSION
# let yf = Owl_fft.D.fft y;;
val yf : (Complex.t, Bigarray.complex64_elt) Owl_dense_ndarray_generic.t =

             C0                      C1                       C2                         C597                    C598                     C599
R (5.02734, 0i) (5.03096, 8.16436E-14i) (5.04187, -1.90459E-13i) ... (5.06014, -2.24884E-13i) (5.04187, 1.92987E-13i) (5.03096, -8.12175E-14i)

Each complex coefficient represents one frequency bin. We can plot its magnitude, represented by z in the code below; these are unnormalised FFT magnitudes, not the amplitudes of the original sinusoids.

OCAML SESSION
# let z = Dense.Ndarray.Z.(abs yf |> re);;
val z : Owl.Dense.Ndarray.Z.cast_arr =

       C0      C1      C2        C597    C598    C599
R 5.02734 5.03096 5.04187 ... 5.06014 5.04187 5.03096

Finally, we plot the result using the code below. The plot is shown in Fig. 7.1c. This plot uses all 600 bins on the axis kfs∕n. Values above 400 Hz represent wrapped negative frequencies: the peaks near 720 and 750 Hz mirror the components at 80 and 50 Hz. The bin spacing is 800∕600 Hz, so 50 Hz lies between bins and its energy spreads into neighbouring bins.

OCAML
let h = Plot.create "plot_sine_3.pdf" in
let frequency = Arr.mul_scalar (Arr.sequential [|int_of_float n|]) (1. /. (n *. t)) in
Plot.set_xlabel h "frequency (Hz)";
Plot.set_ylabel h "FFT magnitude";
Plot.plot ~h frequency z;
Plot.output h;;

The other two functions, rfft and irfft, handle real-valued signals: rfft transforms real input into a complex half-spectrum, and irfft reconstructs real output from that spectrum. Using them can sometimes make code cleaner. For example, we can apply rfft directly to a real ndarray rather than first casting it to a complex array, and apply irfft to the result to recover the real input. The odd-length smoothing example below uses the provided irfft_exact helper.

7.3 Applications of FFTs

There are numerous applications of the FFT, but we pick three here to demonstrate the power of FFT using OCaml. The first is to find a period in a synthetic sunspot-like series, and the second is about identifying dialled digits from audio. Both are inspired by examples in Moler [12]. The third is about image processing. Together these applications demonstrate the wide usage of FFT in various scenarios.

7.3.1 Finding the Period of Sunspots

On the Sun’s photosphere, sunspots appear as spots darker than the surrounding areas, and their number changes according to a certain cycle. Measured sunspot data are available from SILSO [13]. Here we use a synthetic annual series labelled from 1700 to 2020, with an injected 11-year cycle, varying amplitude and small noise. This provides a reproducible example of period detection; it is not an estimate from observations of the Sun.

OCAML
let data = Owl_io.read_csv ~sep:';' "sunspot_full.csv";;
let data = Array.map (fun x -> Array.map float_of_string x)
  data |> Mat.of_arrays;;
let x = Mat.get_slice [[];[0]] data;;
let y = Mat.get_slice [[];[1]] data;;

We can visualise the data x (year) and y (synthetic count) as in Fig. 7.2.

The figure suggests a cycle of about 10 years, but what period does the strongest spectral peak indicate? Let’s start by applying the FFT to this synthetic signal. This will show which periodic component is the most prominent. The helper uses rfft and discards bin zero, which stores the sum of the samples with the default normalisation. It retains the positive-frequency magnitudes; selecting this half-spectrum does not halve the frequencies.

OCAML
let get_frequency y =
  let spectrum = Owl_fft.D.rfft ~axis:0 y in
  let bins = (Dense.Ndarray.Z.shape spectrum).(0) in
  let selected = Dense.Ndarray.Z.get_slice [[1;bins-1];[]] spectrum in
  Dense.Ndarray.Z.(abs selected |> re);;
let get_frequency = get_frequency;;

The frequency (cycle/year) as a unit of measurement seems a bit confusing. To make the cycle easier to interpret, we also plot the FFT magnitude as a function of years/cycle. Both are plotted with code below.

OCAML
let plot_sunspot_freq ~samples p =
  let n = Mat.row_num p in
  let frequency = Mat.of_array
    (Array.init n (fun k -> float_of_int (k+1) /. float_of_int samples)) n 1 in
  let h = Plot.create ~m:1 ~n:2 "plot_sunspot_freq.png" in
  Plot.subplot h 0 0;
  Plot.set_xlabel h "cycles/year";
  Plot.set_ylabel h "FFT magnitude";
  Plot.plot ~h frequency p;
  Plot.subplot h 0 1;
  Plot.set_xlabel h "years/cycle";
  Plot.plot ~h (Mat.scalar_div 1. frequency) p;
  Plot.set_xrange h 0. 40.;
  Plot.output h;;
let p = get_frequency y;;
plot_sunspot_freq ~samples:(Mat.row_num y) p;;

The result is shown in Fig. 7.3. The strongest FFT bin corresponds to about 11.1 years, close to the injected 11-year period. The finite sample length limits the frequency resolution.

7.3.2 Determining the Tone

When we dial a phone number, the sound wave can be seen as a signal. In this example, we show how to decipher which number is dialled according to the given soundwave. This example uses a synthesized 11-digit sequence, 12345678901. Each digit has 5000 tone samples followed by 1000 silent samples, at a sampling rate of 8192 Hz. Let’s first load and visualise them.

OCAML
let fs = 8192.;;
let data = Owl_io.read_csv ~sep:',' "touchtone.csv";;
let data = Array.map (fun x -> Array.map float_of_string x)
           data |> Mat.of_arrays;;
let data = Mat.div_scalar data 128.;;

The generator specifies a sampling rate (fs) of 8192. We have a segment of signal that shows a sequence of synthesized touch tones. We can visualise the signal:

OCAML
let tone_times = Mat.div_scalar (Mat.sequential 1 (Arr.shape data).(1)) fs;;

The result is shown in the left subfigure of Fig. 7.4. The 11 dense segments correspond to the 11 synthesized digits. We can recover the two frequencies in each segment and check which digit they identify.

Each touch tone combines two different frequencies: one from a low-frequency group and one from a high-frequency group. The 11 digits in this sequence use seven frequencies from the 12-key keypad shown in Tbl. 7.2. These combinations are specified for dual-tone multi-frequency signalling (DTMF) in ITU-T Recommendation Q.23 [14]. The full scheme also includes a fourth high-frequency column for keys A–D, which this example does not use. Therefore, we can use FFT to decompose the soundwave for each digit into its two basic frequencies, and check this table to find out the answer. Let’s start by applying the FFT to the original data.

OCAML
let yf = Owl_fft.D.rfft data;;
let y' = Dense.Ndarray.Z.(abs yf |> re);;
let n = (Arr.shape y').(1);;
let x' = Mat.linspace 0. (fs /. 2.) n;;

We plot y’ against x’ similarly using the previous plotting function, and the result is shown in the right side of Fig. 7.4.

We can use the first tone as an example to find out the two frequencies from which it is composed. Let’s start by getting a subset of the signal:

OCAML
let data2 = Arr.get_slice [[];[0; 4999]] data;;

We then perform the same process as before producing the results shown in Fig. 7.5. It shows that the first digit is mainly composed of two frequencies, about 697 and 1209 Hz. Looking them up in Tbl. 7.2, we find that the first digit is 1. You can verify the remaining digits by repeating the same procedure.

7.3.3 Image Processing

FFT remains a powerful tool as the dimensionality of data increases. It can be used for a wide range of image processing tasks such as blurring, compression or denoising. In this section, we demonstrate an image denoising example. The basic idea is similar to the preceding case: an image can be decomposed into two-dimensional spatial frequency components. Here we use a low-pass filter to suppress rapid variations. This can reduce noise, but high spatial frequencies also carry edges and fine detail, so removing them blurs the image; small coefficients do not necessarily represent noise.

As input, we use a cat image as shown in Fig. 7.6a. As a tool for image processing in OCaml, we use the imageUtils.ml script which reads images of PPM format into an ndarray, or saves an ndarray into PPM image. The script is included in the code repository of this book.

OCAML
#use "imageUtils.ml";;
module N = Dense.Ndarray.D;;
module C = Dense.Ndarray.Z;;

As a first step we read the image into an ndarray using the function load_ppm. Since this is a grayscale image, we need only process one single channel of this array, which is a matrix having all elements in the range 0 to 255.

OCAML
let img_arr = load_ppm "cat_noise.ppm" |> Dense.Ndarray.Generic.cast_s2d
  |> N.get_slice [[];[];[0]];;
let shp = N.shape img_arr;;
let h, w = shp.(0), shp.(1);;
let img = N.reshape img_arr [|h; w|]
  |> Dense.Ndarray.Generic.cast_d2z;;

The next step is simple: applying the fft2 function on the image matrix. This function performs a 2-dimensional FFT on the matrix, i.e. it performs FFT on the input matrix twice, once horizontally, and once vertically. The magnitudes of the resulting frequency coefficients can be visualised as in Fig. 7.7a. This surface contains contributions from both the image and its noise.

OCAML
let img_fft = Owl_fft.D.fft2 img;;
visualise_img img_fft "img_fft1.pdf";;

We can apply different kinds of filters on this frequency map img_fft to remove unwanted frequencies. We choose to use a simple one that keeps only the frequencies on the four “corners” of this matrix, setting the rest to zero. In the unshifted FFT layout, these corners contain low spatial frequencies of both signs. We can achieve this with some slicing techniques.

OCAML
let sub_length x frac =
  (float_of_int x) *. frac |> int_of_float;;

let h1 = sub_length h 0.1;;
let h2 = sub_length h 0.9;;
let w1 = sub_length w 0.1;;
let w2 = sub_length w 0.9;;
let index_0 = [ R [h1; h2]; R []];;
let index_1 = [ R [0; h1]; R [w1; w2] ];;
let index_2 = [ R [h2; h-1]; R [w1; w2] ];;
let slice_0 = C.get_fancy index_0 img_fft;;
let slice_1 = C.get_fancy index_1 img_fft;;
let slice_2 = C.get_fancy index_2 img_fft;;

let _ = C.set_fancy index_0 img_fft
  (C.shape slice_0 |> C.zeros);;
let _ = C.set_fancy index_1 img_fft
  (C.shape slice_1 |> C.zeros);;
let _ = C.set_fancy index_2 img_fft
  (C.shape slice_2 |> C.zeros);;
visualise_img img_fft "img_fft2.pdf";;

After this process, the frequency map becomes Fig. 7.7b. Finally, let’s apply the reverse 2D FFT on the processed frequency map, and save the result as an image.

OCAML
let img = Owl_fft.D.ifft2 img_fft |> C.re;;
let image = N.stack ~axis:2 [|img; img; img|];;
let image = N.expand image 4 |> Dense.Ndarray.Generic.cast_d2s;;
let _ = save_ppm_from_arr image "cat_denoise.ppm";;

As shown in Fig. 7.6b, the output has less visible noise and retains the broad features of the cat, but it also loses fine detail and looks blurry.

7.4 Filtering

In Chap. 5, we introduced the generic filter operation, which selects elements according to a predicate. Signal-processing filters instead modify signal values; the following examples use weighted combinations of neighbouring samples or frequency components. A filter is a device or process that removes unwanted components from a signal. Generally, any system that modifies input signals in certain ways is a filter. In this section, we introduce how FFT can be applied to perform some filtering tasks with examples.

7.4.1 Example: Smoothing

Let’s start with smoothing, a common and quite simple filtering task. Suppose we have a segment of noisy signal shaped like a stock price. In many cases we would like to remove rapid fluctuations and see a longer-term trend. The second-edition file goog.csv contains 251 synthetic observations with a slow trend, periodic components and small noise. It uses the familiar price-table layout for this example; it does not contain Google quotations. We can load the data into a matrix called “data” using code below:

OCAML
let data = Owl_io.read_csv ~sep:',' "goog.csv";;
let data = Array.map (fun x ->
    Array.map float_of_string (Array.sub x 1 6))
    (Array.sub data 1 (Array.length data-1)) |> Mat.of_arrays;;

After removing the sample index, the data contains six numeric columns: synthetic open, high, low, close, adjusted close, and volume. Here we use the synthetic close values in the fourth column of the matrix.

OCAML
let y = Mat.get_slice [[];[3]] data;;

To compute the moving average of this signal, we create a window with 10 elements. For this example, we only use a very simple filter which takes an average of 10 elements.

OCAML
let filter = Mat.of_array (Array.make 10 0.1 ) 1 10;;
let moving_average_filter = filter;;

We can then slide this filter window along the input signal to smooth the data step by step.

OCAML
let y' = Mat.mapi (fun i _ ->
    let r = Mat.get_fancy [R [i; i+9]; R []] y in
    Mat.dot filter r |> Mat.sum'
  ) (Mat.get_slice [[0; (Arr.shape y).(0) - 10]; []] y);;

Finally, we plot the resulting smoothed data against the original data. The results are shown in Fig. 7.8. The blue dotted line smooths the jagged original stock price line (red), and represents a smoother view of the synthetic series. Each average is plotted at the centre of its ten-sample window.

7.4.2 Gaussian Filter

The moving average gives equal weight to each element of the window. To change the smoothing profile, we can change this simple filter to another: the Gaussian filter [15]. Instead of giving equal weight to each element in the moving window, the Gaussian filter uses weights proportional to a Gaussian:

p(x) = e−x2 2σ2 . (7.4)

The code below generates a simple 1-D Gaussian filter and normalises the weights to sum to one. The window extends to approximately four standard deviations on either side of its centre. With σ = 3 sample intervals, radius is 12 and the kernel contains 25 weights.

OCAML
let gaussian_kernel sigma =
  if not (Float.is_finite sigma && sigma > 0.) then invalid_arg "positive finite sigma";
  let radius = int_of_float (4. *. sigma +. 0.5) in
  let x = Mat.linspace (-.float_of_int radius) (float_of_int radius) (2*radius+1) in
  let kernel = Mat.map (fun a -> exp (-0.5 *. a *. a /. (sigma *. sigma))) x in
  Mat.div_scalar kernel (Mat.sum' kernel);;
let gaussian_kernel = gaussian_kernel;;
let filter = gaussian_kernel 3.;;

Computing the correlation between the filter and input data as before, we get a smoothed curve in Fig. 7.9.

Filters can be described in both the time and frequency domains. In the time domain, the moving-average and Gaussian filters above combine neighbouring samples. In the frequency domain, their frequency responses describe how they change different frequency components. These are complementary descriptions, not mutually exclusive classes. Other designs, such as windowed-sinc and Chebyshev filters, can be chosen for particular frequency-response requirements [16]. There are many types of filters, each with different shape and application scenario, and we cannot fully cover them here. Please refer to some classical textbooks on signal processing such as Smith [17] for more information.

7.4.3 Signal Convolution

So far we have not used FFT functions to perform filtering. In this section we will demonstrate how they can be applied to solve our synthetic price-series smoothing problem. But first, we need to explain the idea of convolution. For discrete signals, it combines two sequences as follows:

(f ∗ g)[t] = ∑ τ=−∞∞f[τ]g[t − τ] (7.5)

In Eq. 7.5, t and τ are integer sample indices and operator ∗ denotes convolution, and you can think of f as a discrete input signal with g as the filter. The sliding dot products used above compute cross-correlation. Because the moving-average and Gaussian kernels are symmetric, they also give the corresponding valid convolution values. Computing each convolution output requires summing products over the overlapping samples. Direct computation can become expensive for long signals and kernels; continuous convolution uses an integral instead of this sum.

The FFT can reduce the cost of convolution for sufficiently long inputs and kernels. For finite sequences, multiplication of equal-length DFTs corresponds to circular convolution. To obtain linear convolution, pad both inputs with zeros to a common length of at least N + M − 1, where N and M are their lengths [17]. With this padding, the convolution theorem gives:

DFT(f ∗ g) = DFT(f) ⋅DFT(g). (7.6)

To put Eq. 7.6 into plain words: to obtain the DFT of two signals’ convolution, we can simply get the DFT of each signal separately and then multiply them element-wise. That is, convolution in the time domain corresponds to multiplication in the frequency domain. Once you have the DFT(f ∗ g), you can simply apply the inverse transform to get f ∗ g.

For the following smoothing example, we specify a filter directly in the frequency domain by retaining low-frequency bins. This is a different filter from the ten-point moving average. Without zero-padding, it treats the finite series as periodic and corresponds to circular convolution with the inverse DFT of the frequency mask. Let’s first move the data to the frequency domain:

OCAML
let yf = Owl_fft.D.rfft ~axis:0 y;;

The resulting data yf looks like this:

OCAML SESSION
# yf;;
- : (Complex.t, Bigarray.complex64_elt) Owl_dense_ndarray_generic.t =

                        C0
  R0         (27295.2, 0i)
  R1  (-10.0945, 699.605i)
  R2  (-12.0475, 351.714i)
                       ...
R123  (-1.82098, 2.78879i)
R124  (-13.395, -4.45041i)
R125 (-11.4182, -5.74908i)

We keep the first five frequency bins, including the zero-frequency component, setting the rest to zero.

OCAML
let n = (Dense.Ndarray.Z.shape yf).(0);;
let z = Dense.Ndarray.Z.zeros [|n-5; 1|];;
let _ = Dense.Ndarray.Z.set_slice [[5;n-1];[]] yf z;;

Then, we apply reverse FFT on this processed frequency vector. The book helper irfft_exact reconstructs the conjugate spectrum and retains the original number of samples, including an odd length; the current Owl real-inverse entry rejects odd lengths even when the output length is specified:

OCAML
let y2 = irfft_exact ~axis:0 ~n:(Mat.row_num y) yf;;

As with the previous two methods, we can check how the smoothing approach works by plotting the filtered signal. Fig. 7.10 shows the result of retaining only these low frequencies. It is smooth, but is not necessarily a better estimate of the trend: the cutoff determines what is retained, and the periodic assumption can distort the ends of the series.

7.4.4 FFT and Image Convolution

You might have already come across the concept of “convolution” in another context. Indeed, convolution is a core operation in convolutional neural networks (CNNs). In CNNs, it is often applied to multidimensional arrays, but the basic process is similar to what we have described in the previous example. Starting with an ndarray input, another smaller ndarray called “kernel” slides over the input step by step. At each position, an element-wise multiplication and summation are applied, and the result is filled into corresponding position in an output ndarray. This process is illustrated in Fig. 7.11.

Owl has thorough support for convolution operations, including conv1d, conv2d, and conv3d. The numbers refer to one, two, or three spatial dimensions; the arrays also have batch and channel axes. Related operations include dilated and transposed convolutions and the derivatives needed for backpropagation.

It’s totally OK if none of this makes sense to you for now. We will explain the convolution operations and their usage in neural networks in great detail in Chapter 11. The point is that the sliding-kernel operation extends to higher dimensions. Strictly, the neural-network convention used by Owl’s conv1d is cross-correlation: the kernel is not reversed as it is in mathematical convolution. For our symmetric moving-average kernel the distinction does not change the result. We can thus use conv1d to solve the previous smoothing problem:

OCAML
let y3 = Arr.reshape y [|1; Mat.row_num y; 1|];;
let f3 = Arr.reshape moving_average_filter [|Arr.numel moving_average_filter;1;1|];;
let y3' = Arr.conv1d ~padding:VALID y3 f3 [|1|];;

If you are interested in checking the result, the vector y3’ contains the data to plot a smoothed curve. The smoothed data agrees, up to round-off, with that in Fig. 7.8 since the calculation is essentially the same, albeit obtained with much less code. We select VALID padding and the original moving-average kernel explicitly, so that the output agrees with the fully overlapping windows used above.

FFT is a popular implementation method for convolutions. There has been a lot of research on optimising and comparing its performance with other implementation methods, with practical considerations such as kernel size and implementation details of code [18, 19, 20]. We omit these technical discussions here.

7.5 Summary

This chapter revolves around a fundamental idea in signal processing: the Fourier Transform. We started with its definition, then introduced a crucial idea behind its efficient implementation, namely the Fast Fourier Transform. Owl provides FFT support through its PocketFFT backend. We showed how the FFT functions can be used in OCaml, first with some simple examples, then with three applications: recovering a cycle from a synthetic sunspot-like series, deciphering synthesized dial tones, and de-noising an image. Next, we discussed filtering in signal processing using different techniques, including simple averaging smoothing, Gaussian filtering, and FFT-based filtering. Finally we explained the relationship between the two most crucial computations in numerical applications: FFT and convolution. More about the application of convolution in neural networks will be discussed in Chapter 11 of this book.
